definition: famous or well known for something bad

hero.text: The Shadow Thief was notorious for stealing museum paintings, and every hero in the city knew her name.

everyday: That intersection is notorious for traffic jams during rush hour.

contrast.nonExample: The scientist was famous for discovering a cure that saved millions of lives.
contrast.explanation: Notorious means well known for something bad. Being known for saving lives is good fame, so a word like celebrated fits instead.

items.prompt: Which thing is notorious?

options.text: a bakery loved for its fresh bread
a quiet street nobody has heard of
a teacher admired for her kindness
a pirate known across the seas for raiding ships

items.hint: Look for something widely known for something bad.
items.explanation: The pirate is widely known for raiding ships, a bad thing. That makes him notorious.

wrong.a: The bakery is famous for something good.
wrong.b: Nobody has heard of it, so it isn't well known at all.
wrong.c: Kindness is a good reason to be known.

items.prompt: Which word best fits the sentence?
items.passage: The swamp was ___ among early settlers for its clouds of mosquitoes and the fevers that followed.
items.clue: clouds of mosquitoes and the fevers
items.hint: Being known for mosquitoes and fevers is bad fame.
items.explanation: The swamp was well known for bad things, mosquitoes and fevers, so notorious fits best. Famous is possible but neutral; notorious adds the negative tone the clues call for.

wrong.c: Famous is neutral; notorious captures the negative tone better.
wrong.b: Celebrated means praised, which doesn't fit fevers.
wrong.d: It was well known among settlers.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: Al Capone ran a criminal empire in 1920s Chicago. Newspapers wrote about his crimes so often that he became one of the most ___ gangsters in American history.
items.clue: criminal empire; wrote about his crimes so often
items.hint: He was very well known, and for something bad.
items.explanation: Capone was widely known because of his crimes. Well known for something bad is notorious.

wrong.c: Newspapers wrote about him constantly, so he wasn't forgotten.
wrong.d: Admired suggests praise for good deeds.

items.prompt: Which line uses "notorious" correctly?

options.text: "Our coach is notorious for helping every player improve!"
"This notorious blanket is soft and warm."
"Watch out for that printer; it's notorious for jamming at the worst moment."
"She was so notorious that nobody had ever heard of her."

items.hint: Notorious means well known for something bad.
items.explanation: The printer is known for a bad habit, jamming, so notorious fits. Helping players is a good thing, which doesn't match notorious.

wrong.a: Helping players is good; notorious is for bad reputations.
wrong.d: Notorious people are well known, so this contradicts itself.
wrong.b: A soft blanket has no bad reputation.

items.prompt: Which word is closest in meaning to "notorious" in this sentence?
items.passage: The website became notorious for spreading false health advice.
items.hint: Look for the word that means well known for something bad.
items.explanation: Infamous means well known for something bad, just like notorious. Popular means liked by many, which misses the negative meaning.

wrong.a: Popular is positive or neutral; notorious is negative.
wrong.b: Respected is the opposite.

definition: a beginner; someone new to an activity who has little experience

hero.text: As a novice at flying, Juniper wobbled through the air and crash-landed in a hedge.

everyday: The ski school has a gentle slope just for novices.

contrast.nonExample: Mrs. Chen has taught violin for forty years and has won many awards.
contrast.explanation: A novice is a beginner. Someone with forty years of experience is an expert.

items.prompt: Is Theo a novice?
items.passage: Theo just got his first skateboard yesterday and can't ride without holding his dad's hand.
items.hint: Is Theo new and inexperienced?
items.explanation: Yes. Theo just started and can't ride alone yet. A novice is a beginner with little experience.

items.prompt: The root nov means "new," as in novel and renovate. A novice is most likely someone who is…
items.hint: Think "new."
items.explanation: Nov means new, so a novice is new to something, a beginner. A novel is a book, but that meaning doesn't fit a person.

wrong.b: A novel is a book, but a novice isn't a writer.
wrong.c: Old and wise is the opposite of new.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: The chess tournament has two sections. Players who have competed for years enter the open section, while first-time players compete in the ___ section.
items.clue: first-time players; while
items.hint: "While" signals a contrast with experienced players.
items.explanation: "While" contrasts players who have competed for years with first-time players. Beginners are novices.

wrong.d: Veterans are experienced, the opposite of first-time.
wrong.a: Experts are the experienced players.

items.prompt: Which word best describes Maya?
items.passage: Maya has played piano for six months. She can read simple music and play a few songs, but she still makes many mistakes and has never performed for an audience.
items.clue: six months; still makes many mistakes; never performed
items.hint: She has learned some, but she is still early on.
items.explanation: After six months with many mistakes and no performances, Maya is still a beginner: a novice. A virtuoso is a highly skilled performer.

wrong.a: A virtuoso is a master, far beyond Maya's level.
wrong.c: Professionals perform; Maya never has.

items.prompt: Which word is most nearly the OPPOSITE of "novice" in this sentence?
items.passage: Even as a novice reporter, she asked sharp questions that impressed the editors.
items.hint: What do you call someone with many years of experience?
items.explanation: A veteran has lots of experience, the opposite of a novice. Rookie is a synonym.

wrong.b: Rookie means nearly the same as novice.
wrong.a: A student is also still learning.

definition: no longer used because something newer or better has replaced it

hero.text: Pixel's old radio became obsolete once the academy gave every hero a holo-watch.

everyday: Floppy disks are obsolete; today people save files to the cloud or USB drives.

contrast.nonExample: Pencils are old, but students still use them every day.
contrast.explanation: Obsolete means no longer used. Something can be old and still in use, like pencils.

items.prompt: What does "obsolete" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: Once cars became common, horse-drawn carriages quickly became obsolete in most cities.
items.hint: What happened to carriages when cars replaced them?
items.explanation: Cars replaced carriages, so people stopped using them. Obsolete means no longer used because something newer took over.

wrong.a: The sentence is about being replaced, not cost.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: For centuries, sailors navigated by the stars using a tool called a sextant. Today, satellite GPS has made the sextant nearly ___ for everyday navigation.
items.clue: Today, satellite GPS has made
items.hint: GPS replaced the sextant. What happens to replaced tools?
items.explanation: GPS replaced the sextant, so it's rarely used now. Obsolete means no longer used because something better came along.

wrong.b: Essential is the opposite; GPS replaced it.
wrong.d: Accuracy isn't the point; being replaced is.

items.prompt: Is this item obsolete?
items.passage: Grandma's cast-iron pan is sixty years old, and she still cooks eggs in it every morning.
items.hint: Old isn't the same as obsolete. Is the pan still used?
items.explanation: No. The pan is old but still used every day. Obsolete means no longer used because something has replaced it.

items.prompt: Which word best fits the sentence?
items.passage: The library still lends out DVDs, but fewer people borrow them each year. They are becoming ___, though they are not completely gone yet.
items.clue: not completely gone yet; fewer people … each year
items.hint: Which word describes something on its way out but still used?
items.explanation: DVDs are still borrowed, just less, so they're outdated, behind the times. Obsolete is stronger: no longer used at all. The clue "not completely gone yet" rules out obsolete and extinct.

wrong.c: Obsolete means no longer used; DVDs are still borrowed, just less.
wrong.a: Extinct means completely gone.
wrong.d: Fewer people want them, so they're becoming less valuable.

items.prompt: Which word is most nearly the OPPOSITE of "obsolete" in this sentence?
items.passage: Some scientists once believed in a substance called "ether" that filled space, but that theory is now obsolete.
items.hint: What is the opposite of no longer used?
items.explanation: Current means in use now, the opposite of obsolete. Incorrect explains why the ether theory was dropped, but it isn't the opposite of obsolete.

wrong.b: The theory was incorrect, but incorrect describes truth, not whether something is still in use.
wrong.a: Ancient leans toward obsolete, not away from it.

definition: common or widespread in a certain place or time

hero.text: Litter was prevalent in the park until Rex organized a weekly cleanup.

everyday: Colds are more prevalent in winter, when people spend more time indoors together.

contrast.nonExample: Only three people in the whole country have ever seen this rare orchid.
contrast.explanation: Prevalent means common or widespread. Something seen by only three people is rare.

items.prompt: Are sneakers prevalent at this school?
items.passage: At Lincoln Middle School, nearly every student wears sneakers to class every day.
items.hint: Are sneakers common there?
items.explanation: Yes. Nearly every student wears them, so sneakers are widespread at the school. That is prevalent.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: In the 1800s, diseases like cholera were ___ in crowded cities with dirty water. After cities built clean water systems, the number of cases dropped sharply.
items.clue: crowded cities with dirty water; dropped sharply
items.hint: If cases dropped sharply later, how common were they before?
items.explanation: Cases dropped sharply after clean water arrived, so the disease must have been widespread before. That is prevalent.

wrong.a: If cases dropped sharply, they weren't rare before.
wrong.c: Cholera was deadly, not harmless.

items.prompt: Which word is closest in meaning to "prevalent" in this sentence?
items.passage: The belief that the sun moved around Earth was prevalent in Europe for over a thousand years.
items.hint: How many people held this belief?
items.explanation: Widespread means held by many, matching prevalent. The belief was common but not correct, so correct is a trap.

wrong.b: Prevalent is about how common something is, not whether it is true.
wrong.d: It lasted a thousand years, so it wasn't new.

items.prompt: Which word best fits the sentence?
items.passage: Smartphones are not just found in a few homes; in many countries, they are ___ among adults and teenagers alike.
items.clue: not just found in a few homes; alike
items.hint: You need a word meaning very common.
items.explanation: "Not just found in a few homes" calls for a word meaning very common, which is prevalent. Scattered and occasional suggest only some places or times.

wrong.a: Scattered suggests only here and there.
wrong.b: Occasional means sometimes, not everywhere.

items.prompt: Based on the survey, which statement is true?
items.passage: A survey of 500 students found that 430 said they felt tired in the morning, while only 12 said they had trouble finding their classes.

options.text: Getting lost is prevalent among the students.
Morning tiredness is prevalent among the students.

items.clue: 430 said they felt tired
items.hint: Which problem did most students report?
items.explanation: 430 out of 500 students report tiredness, so it is widespread, or prevalent. Only 12 got lost, which is uncommon.

wrong.a: Only 12 of 500 got lost, which is rare.

definition: to prove that a statement or argument is wrong, using evidence

hero.text: When the villain claimed the bridge was safe, Kai refuted him by showing photos of the cracked supports.

everyday: In the debate, Sofia refuted her opponent's claim by quoting the actual statistics.

contrast.nonExample: Jake disagreed with his sister's claim by saying, "Nuh-uh, that's wrong!" over and over.
contrast.explanation: To refute is to prove something wrong with evidence. Just saying "that's wrong" disagrees but proves nothing.

items.prompt: Who refutes the claim "Goldfish only remember things for three seconds"?

options.text: Ava says, "I don't like that idea."
Marcus repeats the claim to his class.
Dr. Patel shows a study where goldfish remembered a feeding signal for months.

items.hint: Who uses evidence to prove the claim wrong?
items.explanation: Dr. Patel uses evidence, a study, to prove the claim false. That is refuting it. Just disliking an idea doesn't disprove it.

wrong.a: Disliking a claim doesn't prove it wrong.
wrong.b: Repeating it supports it.

items.prompt: Which word best describes what the scientist did?
items.passage: People once believed that maggots appeared on rotting meat out of nowhere. Francesco Redi covered some jars of meat and left others open. Maggots appeared only in the open jars, where flies could lay eggs.
items.clue: Maggots appeared only in the open jars
items.hint: He didn't just say the belief was wrong. He proved it with an experiment.
items.explanation: Redi's experiment proved the old belief wrong with evidence, so he refuted it. Denied would mean only saying it was false, without proof.

wrong.b: Denying is just saying something is false; Redi proved it with an experiment.
wrong.c: His results went against the belief.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: The company claimed its new phone battery lasted three days. But a team of reviewers ran the phone nonstop and found it died after just twenty hours, which ___ the company's claim.
items.clue: found it died after just twenty hours
items.hint: The test showed the claim was false.
items.explanation: Twenty hours is far less than three days, so the test showed the claim was wrong, using evidence. That is refuting it.

wrong.a: The results went against the claim.
wrong.c: The reviewers tested the claim; they didn't advertise it.

items.prompt: Did Omar refute the claim?
items.passage: Someone said, "The Great Wall of China is easy to see from the Moon." Omar replied, "I just don't believe it," and walked away.
items.hint: Did Omar use evidence to prove the claim wrong?
items.explanation: No. Omar disagreed but gave no evidence. To refute a claim, you must prove it wrong, for example by citing astronauts who said the Wall can't be seen with the naked eye from the Moon.

items.prompt: Which word is most nearly the OPPOSITE of "refute" in this sentence?
items.passage: The lawyer hoped the new fingerprint evidence would refute the claim that her client was at the scene.
items.hint: What is the opposite of proving something wrong?
items.explanation: Confirm means to show something is true, the opposite of refute. Disprove is a synonym. Question is weaker but leans the same way as refute.

wrong.a: Disprove means nearly the same as refute.
wrong.b: Questioning leans toward refuting, not the opposite.

definition: to make stronger, either physically or by adding support or evidence

hero.text: Bolt reinforced the old dam with steel beams before the flood arrived.

everyday: The new study reinforced the idea that sleep helps memory.

contrast.nonExample: Removing the bottom blocks made the tower so wobbly that it fell over.
contrast.explanation: To reinforce is to strengthen. Removing support weakens something, the opposite.

items.prompt: Is the builder reinforcing the shelf?
items.passage: The bookshelf sagged in the middle, so the builder added a metal bracket underneath to hold it up.
items.hint: Is the bracket making the shelf stronger?
items.explanation: Yes. The bracket adds support so the shelf is stronger. That is reinforcing it.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: Jada's essay argued that school gardens improve nutrition. To ___ her argument, she added data showing that students in garden programs ate twice as many vegetables.
items.clue: added data showing
items.hint: What does adding evidence do to an argument?
items.explanation: Adding supporting data makes the argument stronger. Reinforce means to strengthen, and it works for arguments as well as buildings.

wrong.a: Supporting data makes an argument stronger, not weaker.
wrong.b: Adding data makes the essay longer, not shorter.

items.prompt: Which word is most nearly the OPPOSITE of "reinforced" in this sentence?
items.passage: The coach's praise reinforced the team's belief that they could win the championship.
items.hint: What would weaken the team's belief?
items.explanation: Undermined means weakened, the opposite of reinforced. Boosted is a synonym.

wrong.a: Boosted means nearly the same as reinforced.
wrong.c: The belief already existed; the praise made it stronger.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what reinforce means.

chunks.text: a short review quiz the next day.
a week off to forget everything.

items.hint: Which activity would make learning stronger?
items.explanation: A review quiz strengthens what students learned, so it reinforces it. A week off to forget would weaken it.

items.prompt: How does the second discovery affect the theory?
items.passage: Scientists proposed that a giant asteroid wiped out the dinosaurs. Years later, they found a huge crater off the coast of Mexico that was exactly the right age.

options.text: It has nothing to do with the theory.

items.clue: exactly the right age
items.hint: Does finding a crater of the right age support or weaken the asteroid idea?
items.explanation: A crater of exactly the right age is evidence for the asteroid theory, so it makes the theory stronger: it reinforces it. Refutes would mean it proved the theory wrong.

wrong.a: Refuting would prove the theory wrong; this evidence supports it.
wrong.c: The crater supports the same theory rather than replacing it.

definition: able to recover quickly from difficulty or bounce back after being bent or damaged

hero.text: Juniper was resilient: after losing the first round of trials, she trained harder and won the next one.

everyday: The town was resilient after the hurricane; within a year, most homes and shops had been rebuilt.

contrast.nonExample: After one bad grade, Sam gave up on math completely and stopped trying.
contrast.explanation: A resilient person bounces back from setbacks. Giving up after one setback is the opposite.

items.prompt: Which person is the most resilient?

options.text: Nia never tries out for anything, so she never fails.
Cal is cut from the team, practices all summer, and makes it the next year.
Eva quits piano after one hard lesson.
Ty is lucky and never faces problems.

items.hint: Who bounces back after a setback?
items.explanation: Cal faces a setback, keeps working, and recovers. Bouncing back like that is being resilient.

wrong.a: Avoiding challenges isn't the same as recovering from them.
wrong.c: Quitting after one hard lesson is the opposite.
wrong.d: Resilience shows only when you face problems.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: After a wildfire, some forests take a century to recover. But certain pine trees are remarkably ___: their cones actually need fire's heat to open, so new seedlings sprout within months.
items.clue: new seedlings sprout within months; But
items.hint: "But" contrasts them with forests that take a century to recover.
items.explanation: These pines recover within months, unlike forests that take a century. Recovering quickly from damage is being resilient. Flammable means easily burned, which doesn't explain the fast recovery.

wrong.a: Fragile means easily broken, the opposite.
wrong.d: Flammable is about burning, not recovering.

items.prompt: Which word best describes the material?
items.passage: Engineers tested a new rubber for running shoes. They squashed it under heavy weights thousands of times, and every time it sprang right back to its original shape.
items.clue: sprang right back to its original shape
items.hint: Which word means bouncing back after being squashed?
items.explanation: Springing back to shape after being squashed is resilient. Rigid means it wouldn't bend at all, and brittle means it would crack.

wrong.a: Rigid materials don't squash in the first place.
wrong.c: Brittle materials break instead of springing back.

items.prompt: Which line uses "resilient" correctly?

options.text: "Kids are resilient. Give Mia a week, and she'll be settled in at her new school."
"The glass vase was so resilient that it shattered when I touched it."
"He's resilient, so he gives up whenever things get hard."
"This resilient song has a catchy chorus."

items.hint: Look for someone who will bounce back from a change.
items.explanation: The speaker expects Mia to recover quickly from a big change. That is resilient. Shattering and giving up are the opposite.

wrong.b: Shattering at a touch is fragile, not resilient.
wrong.c: Giving up is the opposite of resilient.
wrong.d: A catchy chorus has nothing to do with bouncing back.

items.prompt: Which word is most nearly the OPPOSITE of "resilient" in this sentence?
items.passage: Coral reefs that are resilient can recover from warm-water events, but many reefs are struggling as oceans heat up.
items.hint: What do you call something that is easily damaged and slow to recover?
items.explanation: Fragile means easily damaged, the opposite of resilient. Hardy is a synonym.

wrong.c: Hardy means nearly the same as resilient.
wrong.a: Color has nothing to do with recovering.

definition: thinly spread out; few and far apart

hero.text: Trees were sparse on the rocky hillside, so Kai could spot the lost hiker from far away.

everyday: The desert has sparse plant life: just a cactus here and a shrub there.

contrast.nonExample: The rainforest was so thick with plants that sunlight barely reached the ground.
contrast.explanation: Sparse means thinly spread. A thick, crowded rainforest is dense, the opposite.

items.prompt: Is the crowd sparse?
items.passage: The stadium holds 50,000 people, but only about 200 fans came to the rainy game, scattered across the empty seats.
items.hint: Are the fans few and spread out?
items.explanation: Yes. Two hundred fans scattered across a huge stadium are few and far apart. That is sparse.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: In the far north of Canada, towns are hundreds of miles apart, and some regions have fewer than one person per square mile. The population there is ___.
items.clue: hundreds of miles apart; fewer than one person per square mile
items.hint: Are people packed together or spread far apart?
items.explanation: Towns hundreds of miles apart and less than one person per square mile mean people are thinly spread. That's sparse. Dense is the opposite.

wrong.b: Dense means crowded together, the opposite.
wrong.c: Nothing tells you whether it is growing.

items.prompt: Which word best fits the sentence?
items.passage: The historian wished she had more to work with, but records from the village were ___: just a few letters and one faded map.
items.clue: just a few letters and one faded map
items.hint: There are some records, but only a few.
items.explanation: "Just a few letters and one map" means there is very little. Sparse fits. Missing would mean there were none at all, but a few exist.

wrong.b: Missing means none at all; she has a few records.
wrong.a: Abundant means plentiful, the opposite.
wrong.d: A few letters and one faded map aren't detailed records.

items.prompt: Which word is most nearly the OPPOSITE of "sparse" in this sentence?
items.passage: Grandpa's hair has become sparse on top, but he says it keeps him cool in summer.
items.hint: What is the opposite of thinly spread hair?
items.explanation: Thick means growing closely together, the opposite of sparse. Thin is a synonym.

wrong.c: Thin means nearly the same as sparse.
wrong.b: Hair can be short and still thick.

items.prompt: Which word best describes the decorations in this room?
items.passage: The artist's studio had white walls, one small painting, a single chair, and a plant in the corner. She said empty space helped her think.
items.clue: one small painting, a single chair; empty space
items.hint: How many things are in the room?
items.explanation: With only one painting, one chair, and one plant, the decorations are few and spread out. That's sparse.

wrong.a: The room has lots of empty space.
wrong.c: White walls and few items don't suggest lots of color.

definition: not certain or final; done in a hesitant or trial way

hero.text: The team made a tentative plan to meet at noon, but Pixel said they'd confirm once the storm passed.

everyday: We have tentative plans to visit Grandma in June, but we haven't bought tickets yet.

contrast.nonExample: The tickets are bought, the hotel is booked, and we leave on Friday at 8:00.
contrast.explanation: Tentative means not yet certain. When everything is booked and confirmed, the plan is final.

items.prompt: Which plan is tentative?

options.text: "The concert is Saturday at 7. Here are your tickets."
"Graduation is June 10. It's on the school calendar."
"Practice is at 4, the same as every week."
"Let's say we'll meet Thursday, but I'll text you if that changes."

items.hint: Which plan might still change?
items.explanation: "I'll text you if that changes" shows the plan isn't final. Tentative means not yet certain.

wrong.a: Tickets in hand mean the plan is set.
wrong.b: It's on the official calendar, so it's definite.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: The scientists called their conclusion about the fossil's age ___. They said they would need more tests before announcing a final answer.
items.clue: would need more tests before announcing a final answer
items.hint: The conclusion isn't final yet.
items.explanation: Needing more tests before a final answer means the conclusion is uncertain for now. That is tentative. Definite and permanent mean settled.

wrong.d: Definite means settled, but they need more tests.
wrong.a: Permanent means it won't change; theirs might.

items.prompt: Which word best describes the puppy's steps?
items.passage: The puppy had never seen snow before. It put one paw down, pulled it back, then slowly tried again, sniffing the cold white ground.
items.clue: pulled it back, then slowly tried again
items.hint: The puppy is unsure but still trying. Is it frozen with fear?
items.explanation: Pulling back and slowly trying again shows hesitant, trial steps, which are tentative. Terrified is too strong, since the puppy keeps exploring.

wrong.d: Terrified is too strong; the puppy keeps trying.
wrong.b: Bold steps would be confident, not hesitant.
wrong.c: Clumsy means awkward, not unsure.

items.prompt: Which line uses "tentative" correctly?

options.text: "The date is tentative, so it will never, ever change."
"She gave a tentative smile, unsure whether the new kids would be friendly."
"I'm so tentative that I shouted my answer before anyone else."
"We pitched our tentative in the campground."

items.hint: Tentative describes something hesitant or uncertain.
items.explanation: A tentative smile is hesitant, given when you're unsure. The line explains the uncertainty: "unsure whether the new kids would be friendly."

wrong.a: Tentative means it might change, so this contradicts itself.
wrong.c: Shouting first is confident, not hesitant.

items.prompt: Which word is most nearly the OPPOSITE of "tentative" in this sentence?
items.passage: The two countries signed a tentative agreement, but leaders on both sides still have to approve the details.
items.hint: What is the opposite of not yet settled?
items.explanation: Final means completely settled, the opposite of tentative. Provisional is a synonym meaning temporary until confirmed.

wrong.b: Provisional means nearly the same as tentative.
wrong.a: Whether it is secret is a separate idea.

definition: agreed on by everyone in a group, with no one disagreeing

hero.text: The vote was unanimous: all six heroes chose Nova to lead the mission.

everyday: The jury's verdict was unanimous; all twelve jurors agreed.

contrast.nonExample: The class voted 25 to 3 to go to the science museum.
contrast.explanation: Unanimous means everyone agrees. A strong majority isn't unanimous if even a few people disagree.

items.prompt: Was the decision unanimous?
items.passage: The student council voted on a new recycling program. Eight members voted yes, and one voted no.
items.hint: Did every single member agree?
items.explanation: No. One member voted no, so not everyone agreed. Unanimous means every person agrees, with no one against.

items.prompt: Unanimous comes from Latin parts meaning "one" and "mind." A unanimous group is one that…

options.text: agrees as if with one mind

items.hint: Picture everyone in a group sharing one mind.
items.explanation: "One" + "mind" = everyone thinking the same thing, complete agreement. A unanimous group can have many members.

wrong.a: A unanimous group can be big; everyone just agrees.
wrong.b: A leader deciding alone isn't everyone agreeing.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: In 1954, the Supreme Court ruled in Brown v. Board of Education that school segregation was unconstitutional. The chief justice worked hard so that all nine justices would agree, believing the decision would carry more weight if it were ___.
items.clue: all nine justices would agree
items.hint: What do you call a decision everyone agrees on?
items.explanation: "All nine justices would agree" defines unanimous. A close or divided decision would have some justices disagreeing.

wrong.a: A close decision means nearly split.

items.prompt: Which word best describes the vote?
items.passage: Of the thirty members, twenty-two voted to paint the clubhouse green. Eight wanted blue.
items.clue: Eight wanted blue
items.hint: Most agreed, but did everyone?
items.explanation: Most members chose green, so it was a majority vote. It wasn't unanimous, because eight people disagreed.

wrong.b: Unanimous means everyone; eight people wanted blue.
wrong.c: 22 to 8 isn't a tie.

items.prompt: Which statement shows a unanimous opinion?
items.passage: Food critics tried the new restaurant. Every single critic praised the soup. Most liked the bread. Opinions on the dessert were mixed.
items.clue: Every single critic praised the soup
items.hint: Which dish did every critic like?
items.explanation: "Every single critic" praised the soup, so the praise was unanimous. "Most" liked the bread, which is a majority, not everyone.

wrong.b: Most is not all, so the bread's praise wasn't unanimous.
wrong.a: Opinions on dessert were mixed.
